title: Route 66 Hits 100: The 'Mother Road' That Refused to Fade Away
summary:
It's been called the "Mother Road," a 2,400-mile ribbon of asphalt that carried millions of Americans toward new lives. Now, Route 66 is turning 100 — and it's throwing a party across eight states.

Route 66 was officially established on November 11, 1926. It linked Chicago, Illinois, to Los Angeles, California, stitching together local, state, and national roads. Many were in rough shape at first. By 1938, the entire route was finally paved.

The highway became a symbol of hope during the Great Depression, the severe economic crisis that began in 1929. When drought and massive dust storms destroyed farms across the central U.S., thousands of families drove west on Route 66, searching for jobs and a fresh start.

After World War II, car travel exploded. Roadside diners, motels, gas stations, and bizarre attractions turned the highway into an adventure. Route 66 came to represent freedom itself.

But by the mid-20th century, Americans wanted faster roads. In 1956, the government began building the Interstate Highway System — wider, straighter, and speedier. Those new highways gradually replaced or bypassed Route 66. In 1985, it was officially removed from the U.S. Highway System.

Here's the twist: the road didn't vanish. Preservation groups and communities fought to protect the remaining sections and historic landmarks. Today, Route 66 is a living piece of American history.

Celebrations have been happening all year and will continue through November 11, the official 100th birthday. On September 3, the Main Street of America Road Show began touring a documentary called Route 66: The Main Street of America. It will be shown in communities across all eight states, ending with a grand finale in Los Angeles on November 7, 2026.
why_it_matters: Roads decide where families can move, work and start over, so the highways being built today will shape which towns thrive a hundred years from now.

background_read: Route 66 was one of the first big results of the U.S. Highway System of 1926, when the country finally tried to number and connect its scattered local roads into one national network.

In the 1930s a combination of drought and huge dust storms — remembered as the Dust Bowl — drove hundreds of thousands of farming families out of states like Oklahoma and Arkansas, and many of them headed west on Route 66.

The writer John Steinbeck (an American novelist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature) followed one such family in his 1939 book 'The Grapes of Wrath', and it was Steinbeck who popularised the nickname 'the Mother Road'. A hit song from the 1940s, '(Get Your Kicks on) Route 66', later made the highway a pop-culture legend.

The Interstate Highway System that eventually replaced it was championed by President Dwight D. Eisenhower (the U.S. president in the 1950s, who had been impressed by Germany's fast roads), and Congress approved the funding in 1956. The new highways pulled traffic away, and Route 66 was officially removed from the system in 1985.
Since then, Congress has created a Route 66 Centennial Commission to help plan the anniversary, and stretches of the old road in several states are now marked with 'Historic Route 66' signs.

perspectives.description: Communities along the old route see the centennial as a chance to bring visitors, money and attention to small towns that the Interstates skipped. Historic motels, diners and neon signs become attractions in their own right.

Nostalgia can hide the hardship: the families who drove west during the Dust Bowl were often desperate, and Black travellers on Route 66 faced segregation, relying on guides such as the Negro Motorist Green Book to find places that would serve them.

Route 66 shows a repeating cycle: new technology (canals, then railways, then Interstates) makes older routes obsolete, and decades later people rediscover them as heritage. The road's value shifts from transport to memory.

The next century of Route 66 depends on funding and on how people travel — electric cars, self-driving vehicles and charging stations could change what a roadside stop even looks like. Preservation groups argue the road should be protected as a national historic trail rather than left to local budgets.
